--- ABSTRACT ---
[AIMS]: Brivaracetam (BRV) is an antiepileptic drug in Phase III clinical development. BRV binds to synaptic vesicle 2A (SV2A) protein and is also suggested to inhibit voltage-gated sodium channels (VGSCs). To evaluate whether the effect of BRV on VGSCs represents a relevant mechanism participating in its antiepileptic properties, we explored the pharmacology of BRV on VGSCs in different cell systems and tested its efficacy at reducing the sustained repetitive firing (SRF).
[METHODS]: Brivaracetam investigations on the voltage-gated sodium current (I(Na)) were performed in N1E-155 neuroblastoma cells, cultured rat cortical neurons, and adult mouse CA1 neurons. SRF was measured in cultured cortical neurons and in CA1 neurons. All BRV (100-300 μM) experiments were performed in comparison with 100 μM carbamazepine (CBZ).
[RESULTS]: Brivaracetam and CBZ reduced IN a in N1E-115 cells (30% and 40%, respectively) and primary cortical neurons (21% and 47%, respectively) by modulating the fast-inactivated state of VGSCs. BRV, in contrast to CBZ, did not affect I(Na) in CA1 neurons and SRF in cortical and CA1 neurons. CBZ consistently inhibited neuronal SRF by 75-93%.
[CONCLUSIONS]: The lack of effect of BRV on SRF in neurons suggests that the reported inhibition of BRV on VGSC currents does not contribute to its antiepileptic properties.

key_findings.finding: The key primary comparative study is Margineanu et al., “Brivaracetam differentially affects voltage-gated sodium currents without impairing sustained repetitive firing in neurons,” CNS Neuroscience & Therapeutics (2015), PMID 25444522. It tested BRV at 100–300 μM versus carbamazepine (CBZ) 100 μM in N1E-115 neuroblastoma cells, cultured rat cortical neurons, and adult mouse CA1 neurons; SRF was tested in cultured cortical and CA1 neurons.

source_tools.relevance: Primary paper abstract and experimental systems/concentrations

key_findings.finding: BRV reduced peak voltage-gated Na+ current (INa) in N1E-115 cells by approximately 30% and in primary cortical neurons by approximately 21%, compared with approximately 40% and 47%, respectively, for CBZ. The BRV effect was attributed to modulation of the fast-inactivated state, including a hyperpolarizing shift in half-inactivation voltage at 1, 10, and 100 μM in N1E-115 cells.

source_tools.relevance: Direct quantitative comparison and fast-inactivation result
Detailed results preview on voltage dependence of fast inactivation
Independent annotation of negative correlation with INa

key_findings.finding: The effect was system-dependent: BRV did not affect INa in adult mouse CA1 neurons under the study conditions, whereas CBZ did. Thus the paper supports differential, cell-system-dependent modulation rather than a uniform NaV blockade.

BRV did not impair sustained repetitive firing in either cultured cortical neurons or adult mouse CA1 neurons, despite its INa effects in N1E-115 cells and cortical neurons. In the same assays, CBZ inhibited neuronal SRF by 75–93%. Therefore, the direct comparative evidence supports preserved SRF with BRV, in contrast to the firing impairment produced by CBZ.
